title: Trump Would Face an Uphill Battle Suing The Times Over Its Tax Article
text: Over 20 years ago, a secretly made recording of a cellphone conversation turned up at a radio station in Pennsylvania. Federal law made broadcasting such recordings illegal, but the station put it on the air anyway. The case went to the United States Supreme Court, which ruled in favor of the radio station in 2001. According to legal experts, that decision, Bartnicki v. Vopper, seriously weakens Donald J. Trump's claim that The New York Times could be held liable for publishing parts of his tax returns. Any attempt to punish “publication of truthful information of public concern,” Justice John Paul Stevens wrote for the majority, “implicates the core purposes of the First Amendment.” That holds true even when someone broke the law in passing the information to a news organization, he wrote. “A stranger’s illegal conduct does not suffice to remove the First Amendment shield from speech about a matter of public concern.” Shortly before The Times posted its article on Mr. Trump's taxes, Marc E. Kasowitz, one of his lawyers, sent The Times a letter threatening legal action. Mr. Kasowitz said that “an individual taxpayer’s income tax returns are confidential and statutorily protected from public disclosure.” That is accurate as far as it goes. A few hours later, in an email sent before publication, Mr. Kasowitz wrote that “any unauthorized disclosure, which publication by The New York Times would be, is illegal.” He pointed to a federal law that makes it a crime “willfully to print or publish” federal tax return information. It was the only law he cited. Here, however, things become more complicated. The Times published parts of state tax returns only, from New York, New Jersey and Connecticut. The federal law Mr. Kasowitz cited does not appear to cover state returns.

title: VFW hits back at Obama: Our politics are not 'confused'
text: The country's largest veterans group struck back at President Obama on Thursday, urging him not to “denigrate” its members' intelligence after the president suggested they were easily influenced by cable news and “right-wing radio.” The Veterans of Foreign Wars took the president to task after Obama referred to the political views heard in “VFW halls” during a speech in Indiana on Wednesday that moved back and forth between campaign politics and the economy. “I don’t know how many VFW Posts the president has ever visited, but our near 1.7 million members are a direct reflection of America,” VFW National Commander John A. Biedrzycki Jr. said in a statement. “We don’t have confused politics, we don’t need left or rightwing media filters telling us how to think or vote, and we don’t need any President of the United States lecturing us about how we are individually [affected] by the economy.” Speaking in Elkhart, Ind., Obama had complained about the “primary story” that he said Republicans tell about the economy, one centered on how “moochers at the bottom of the income ladder” are squeezing middle-class families. “We have been hearing this story for decades,” Obama said. “Tales about welfare queens, talking about takers, talking about the ‘47percent.’ It's the story that is broadcast every day on some cable news stations, on right-wing radio, it's pumped into cars, and bars, and VFW halls all across America, and right here in Elkhart.” Obama went on: “And if you're hearing that story all the time, you start believing it. title: Why Your Backyard Chickens Could Be Making You Sick With Salmonella
text: Backyard homesteading has been growing steadily more popular over the past decade. As people, especially those in cities, have learned more about sustainability and ecological living, backyard chickens in particular have turned into a sort of mascot for that lifestyle. Raising chickens is affordable, funky and fun, but it doesn't come without some risks. Live poultry, such as chickens, ducks, geese and turkeys, often carry harmful germs. This year the CDC has reported several cases of Salmonella spreading via backyard chickens. Eight different states are reporting Salmonella outbreaks tied to backyard chickens. These germs live naturally in the intestines of poultry (and plenty of other animals). That means Salmonella germs are present in their droppings and on their bodies (feathers, feet and beaks), even when the birds look healthy and clean. From there the germs can easily get onto cages, coops, food dishes, hay, plants and soil wherever the birds live and roam. They can then pass onto the hands, shoes and clothes of people who handle the birds or their eggs. Although it usually doesn't make the birds sick or show any signs of infection, Salmonella causes serious problems when it is passed on to people. It isn't a question of keeping your chicken coops clean or buying “healthy” chickens. Even organically fed poultry in spotless coops can carry Salmonella, and there's really no way to tell which birds have it. Is Salmonella Serious? A Salmonella infection is no joke: it can bring serious intestinal distress, with symptoms including diarrhea, vomiting, fever and abdominal cramping. If the symptoms are bad enough, an infected person will need to be hospitalized.

title: Three more states reject Trump commission's request for voter data
text: On Monday, Maryland, Delaware and Louisiana became the latest of a growing number of U.S. states to refuse to hand over voter data to a commission President Donald Trump set up to investigate possible voting fraud. Over 20 states, among them Virginia, Kentucky, California, New York and Massachusetts, have declined to supply some or all of the information the panel asked for, saying the request was unnecessary and violated privacy. Trump, a Republican, created the Presidential Advisory Commission on Election Integrity in May after making unsubstantiated claims that millions of people voted illegally for his Democratic rival, Hillary Clinton, in last November's election. Describing the request as “repugnant,” Maryland Attorney General Brian Frosh said in a statement that his office had told the State Board of Elections that the commission's request was illegal. The request “appears designed only to intimidate voters and to indulge President Trump’s fantasy that he won the popular vote,” Frosh said. The commission had sent a letter to the 50 states asking for voter information including names, the last four digits of Social Security numbers, addresses, birth dates, political affiliations, felony convictions and voting histories. Louisiana Secretary of State Tom Schedler said the presidential commission could buy the limited information that is legally available to candidates running for office. “You’re not going to play politics with Louisiana’s voter data,” he said in a statement. Delaware Elections Commissioner Elaine Manlove told Milford's WXDE-FM radio in an interview that her office would not comply because some of the information was confidential. Manlove said she was working with the attorney general's office to see whether the request could be refused entirely. Trump has lashed out at the states that have refused to hand over the data. In a tweet on Saturday he said, “What are they trying to hide?”

title: Juncker unveils new code of conduct for EU Commission members
text: Under a new ethical code of conduct proposed on Wednesday by the President of the European Commission, members of the Commission will have to wait two years before starting new jobs after leaving the EU executive. In a bid to strengthen public trust in the EU institutions, Jean-Claude Juncker called for more strictly enforced ethical standards and greater transparency in the Commission. The code of conduct will take effect from Feb. 1, 2018, and will apply to all current members. It follows the public outcry caused when Juncker's predecessor, Jose Manuel Barroso, joined U.S. investment bank Goldman Sachs to advise it on Brexit, and the reprimand of former Commissioner Neelie Kroes for failing to declare income that would effectively have reduced her pension. The cooling-off period between the end of a Commission term and the start of new employment was lengthened from 18 months to two years for members, and to three years for the president. The code also obliges members to declare investments worth more than 10,000 euro ($11,900) and sets up an Independent Ethical Committee to give advice on all ethical issues.

title: Revived U.S. travel ban causes confusion and anger in Middle East
text: A U.S. Supreme Court ruling that allows President Donald Trump's travel ban to be partly implemented has caused anger and confusion in parts of the Middle East, where would-be visitors are worried about their travel plans and their futures. The blanket 90-day ban on visitors from six Muslim-majority countries, Iran, Libya, Somalia, Sudan, Syria and Yemen, and a 120-day ban on all refugees had been fully blocked by lower courts after Trump issued it on March 6, saying it was needed to prevent terrorism attacks. On Monday, the Supreme Court ruled that the bans could go ahead, but only for foreigners without a “bona fide relationship” with an American person or entity, and it did not specify what that meant. The ruling left some in the Middle East unsure whether they would be able to enter the United States. “It’s a big disappointment for me,” said a 52-year-old Sudanese man in the capital Khartoum, who thought he would now be refused a visa to visit relatives in the United States. The man, who asked not to be identified, said he would not know the result until at least Sunday, when the U.S. Embassy reopens after a series of national holidays. “I’ve traveled to America before and I don’t know why I’m prevented from traveling (now). I didn’t violate American law during my previous visits,” he said. At the U.S. Consulate in Dubai, where a queue of people waiting to process visa applications normally stretches out the door, a reporter saw few people. Middle East airlines have not yet received a directive from the United States following the ruling, industry sources said on Wednesday. U.S. flights would continue to operate normally until guidance is received, the sources said.

title: Study: American Adults Are Having Less Sex Than 25 Years Ago
text: American adults are having less sex than they did a quarter of a century ago, with the steepest decline among married people, according to a new study released on Tuesday. The study, published in the journal Archives of Sexual Behavior, found a decline in sexual activity across gender, race, region, education level and work status. One factor behind the decline is the rising percentage of unpartnered people, who tend to have less sex than people with partners. But a major factor is a steady fall in the rate of sexual activity among people who are married or living with partners. According to data from the General Social Survey, the study found that American adults have sex seven to nine fewer times a year than in the 1990s. In the 1990s the average person had sex 60 to 62 times a year, but by 2014 that figure had fallen to fewer than 53 times a year. Among married people the drop was even steeper, from 73 times a year in 1990 to 55 in 2014. Married people now have sex less often than unmarried people, who have sex an average of 59 times a year. People who are not in couples, including those who were married in the past, have sex half as often as those who are, the study said. The decline in couples supports this finding. Fewer Americans were living with a partner in 2014 than in 1986; in 2014, only 59 percent were, according to GSS data. The report listed possible reasons for the decline in sexual activity, including increased access to entertainment and social media, a decline in happiness among people aged 30 and over, and a higher incidence of depression and of the use of substances associated with sexual dysfunction.

title: Philippines Floats ‘Gentleman’s Agreement’ with China over South China Sea
text: Philippine Foreign Secretary Alan Peter Cayetano proposed on Thursday that the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) should reach a “gentlemen’s agreement” on South China Sea waterways, since there is no legal authority that could enforce a binding contract on navigation in the region. “If it’s legally binding, which court can the parties go to? And the countries that do not comply, will they respect that court?” Cayetano told reporters. “Let’s start with it being binding, gentlemen’s agreement. We have a community of nations that signed it.” He was referring to the draft framework for a South China Sea code of conduct between ASEAN and China on Thursday. Cayetano appeared to be giving up on getting China to sign a tougher contract. As one report delicately puts it, there is “regional skepticism whether Beijing will commit to rules likely to restrain its maritime ambitions.” A “gentleman’s agreement” of this kind would govern shipping lanes that handle five trillion dollars a year in commerce. The proposal comes after President Rodrigo Duterte said China was installing “some kind of armed garrison” on the disputed South China Sea islands it claims. Some of ASEAN's representatives believe China is going along with the draft framework only to “buy time for Beijing to wrap up construction activities,” at which point Chinese ownership of everything Beijing wants in the region would be a fait accompli, according to reports, despite last year's ruling by the Permanent Court of Arbitration in the Hague against Chinese claims of sovereignty. China largely ignored that ruling, which explains Cayetano's doubt that any controlling legal authority capable of enforcing anything stricter than a gentleman's agreement could be found.

title: In A Historic First, ICC Gearing Up To Investigate US War Crimes In Afghanistan
text: The International Criminal Court (ICC) is getting ready to launch a full investigation into potential war crimes in Afghanistan, including those committed by U.S. military personnel, Foreign Policy reported exclusively on Tuesday. The magazine writes: “Multiple sources have indicated that the chief prosecutor, Fatou Bensouda, will seek to initiate an investigation in the coming weeks, likely after the U.S. presidential election but before the end of the year. U.S. officials visited The Hague recently to discuss the potential investigation and to express concerns about its scope.” A formal investigation of U.S. activities would be a first in the history of the ICC, to which the U.S. is not a party. But since Afghanistan is a member, an investigation is “certainly possible,” Phyllis Bennis of the Institute for Policy Studies told Common Dreams. “Afghanistan joined the ICC in 2003, so all actions after that time are subject to ICC jurisdiction,” Bennis said. “But then you get to the question of political will,” Bennis added. The ICC has famously failed to investigate powerful Western nations while prosecuting African dictators, a disparity so glaring that several African countries recently walked out of the court, condemning it as the “International Caucasian Court.” “Is the prosecutor concerned enough about the accusations of discrimination levied against the ICC that she’s willing to go after U.S. clients and U.S. officials?” Bennis asked. Rights advocates are hoping Bensouda may be willing to take on powerful nations. The prosecutor was behind the preliminary ICC report, “Report on Preliminary Examination Activities,” which was published last year.
